**February 29, 1960 — a Monday**

Start with the date itself, because you can't not.

February 29 occurs because the Earth takes 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 46 seconds to orbit the sun. The calendar absorbs the extra fraction every four years. You were born on the absorption day — a date that exists only as a rounding correction, and then only every 1,461 days. In 66 years you have had 16 actual February 29 birthdays. The next is 2028. Every other year of your life, the date you were born on does not appear in the calendar at all.

This creates a mild philosophical problem that no one else has quite the same way: on what day do you actually become a year older? February 28? March 1? Countries split on this. Courts have been asked to rule. You have been navigating the ambiguity since childhood.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, the city of Agadir, Morocco ceased to exist.

At 11:47 PM local time, an earthquake struck. Agadir was a modern coastal resort city, and it collapsed in seconds. Estimates of the dead run from 12,000 to 15,000 — roughly a third of the population. The Moroccan government eventually determined the ruins were beyond salvage and bulldozed the site. A new Agadir was built several kilometers away. The city that stood on February 29, 1960 does not exist anymore.

It is the rarest date on the calendar, and one of the deadliest earthquakes in African history fell on it.

---

**The twenty-six days before your birth and the twenty-one days after describe an arc across Africa** that was unlike anything the continent had seen.

On February 3, 1960 — 26 days before you were born — British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan stood in the parliament of South Africa, in Cape Town, and delivered a speech to an audience of white Afrikaner politicians who were not going to enjoy it. "The wind of change is blowing through this continent," he told them. A British Prime Minister, on South African soil, was serving notice that the age of colonial rule in Africa was ending — and that Britain would not be defending it. The speech was received with stony silence.

Three weeks after your birth, on March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black demonstrators in the township of Sharpeville. The protesters had gathered peacefully to challenge the pass laws requiring Black South Africans to carry identity documents at all times. Sixty-nine people were killed, 180 wounded. Most were shot in the back while fleeing. The South African government declared a state of emergency, banned the ANC and the Pan Africanist Congress, and doubled down on apartheid. International outrage crystallized. The anti-apartheid movement had its defining atrocity.

You were born between Macmillan's warning and Sharpeville's answer to it. The wind of change had been announced; South Africa's government had chosen its response. The resulting struggle would last another 34 years, until Nelson Mandela walked out of prison in 1990.

---

**1960 was the Year of Africa** — seventeen nations gained independence in a single calendar year. The colonial map that had been largely fixed since the 1880s dissolved in twelve months. You were born in the year that transformation peaked.

Elsewhere: in May, the FDA approved the oral contraceptive pill — a decision with consequences for daily life as profound as almost any technology of the century. In September, John Kennedy and Richard Nixon faced each other in the first televised presidential debate; people who heard it on radio thought Nixon had won, people who watched it on television thought Kennedy had. You grew up in the country that debate produced. In November, Kennedy won, by the narrowest popular vote margin in modern American history.

---

**Sixty-six years.**

You were born into the last days of a world where most of Africa was still colonized. You were one when Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space. You were three when Kennedy was shot. You were nine when Apollo 11 landed on the moon and Woodstock happened in the same summer. Vietnam and Watergate shaped your teenage years. You were 30 when Mandela walked free, completing the arc that ran through the three weeks surrounding your birth.

Your 16 actual February 29 birthdays have each landed in a different moment: 1964 (the Civil Rights Act), 1968 (the year everything broke), 1988 (late Reagan), 2000 (Y2K survived), 2020 (the pandemic beginning). Each one a different world wearing the same date.

The next one is 2028. What it will look like is, as always on this particular date, genuinely unknown.
